dedupe_keys.name: sri lanka capacity gaps in post disaster waste management after the indian ocean tsunami

description: This case study examines why disaster waste management was weak in Sri Lanka and how capacity could be built. Gayani Karunasena of the University of Moratuwa and Dilanthi Amaratunga of the University of Salford wrote it as a chapter of the book Recovery from the Indian Ocean Tsunami: A Ten-Year Journey, published by Springer in its Disaster Risk Reduction series. The chapter sets out why disaster waste matters for public health, the environment, rescue and emergency services, lifelines and socio-economic recovery, then reviews the gaps in managing it in developing countries with emphasis on Sri Lanka. The main gaps found were the lack of single point responsibility, no provision for disaster waste in existing policies, and capacity limits in everyday solid waste management; the authors propose a regulatory body with enforceable rules and seven areas for capacity building. The book chapter is sold by Springer, and an author copy is free to read in the University of Huddersfield repository for personal research or study. Coverage is national. Caveats: the analysis is qualitative and draws on the tsunami response and later experience, not quantities. Simulation uses: institutional constraints to represent in scenarios of debris clearance capacity after coastal disasters. Related records: the Great East Japan disposal cost study (case_study-great-east-japan-earthquake-disaster-waste-disposal-cost-efficiency) quantifies costs after another tsunami.
